<reflection>
The first experiment provided initial fitting results with negative log-likelihood (NLL) values for all 20 mechanisms. The NLL values for most mechanisms are very close, with M7 being the best (lowest NLL) and M3 the worst. The small differences (e.g., within ~0.6 NLL for the top 18) indicate that the first experiment alone does not strongly discriminate among the majority of mechanisms. M3 and M5 have noticeably higher NLL (less negative), suggesting they are less plausible, but they still retain some support. The aim of the first experiment was to establish a baseline, which was achieved. However, the limited discrimination power necessitates further experiments to reduce uncertainty over the entire set.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To discriminate among the many plausible mechanisms, we need to probe the dependence on catalyst concentration. Many mechanisms involve dimerization (e.g., M2, M3, M5, M19) or catalyst deactivation steps that may depend on catalyst concentration. Doubling the catalyst concentration from 0.05 M to 0.1 M while keeping substrate at 2.0 M and no product will provide a different regime. If the reaction rate scales linearly with catalyst concentration, simple mechanisms like M1 (Michaelis-Menten with reversible steps) are favored. If there is sublinear or superlinear scaling, mechanisms with dimerization, inhibition, or deactivation may be indicated. This condition avoids extreme saturation (catalyst is still within the moderate range) and should yield a progress curve that can be compared to the first run to extract rate laws. This design is effective because it targets a wide range of mechanisms simultaneously, particularly those sensitive to catalyst concentration, without collapsing mechanistic differences through saturation or depletion.
</hypothesis>
